newsitem.title: MEXICO: Dornbusch says "essential" for Mexico peso to slip.
newsitem.headline: Dornbusch says "essential" for Mexico peso to slip.

text.p: Economist Rudiger Dornbusch said on Wednesday it was "essential" for the Mexican peso to decline over time in tandem with the country's inflation rate.

In an interview with Reuters, the MIT professor said he is comfortable with the current level of the peso, which has declined sharply in recent days and weakened again today after strengthening for much of this year.
But he warned that the currency needs to continue to weaken in line with Mexico's high inflation rate.

"The peso over time has to accompany the rate of inflation. That is what is important. The current level is OK -- not glorious, but not perilous. But that the peso should decline over time, that is essential," Dornbusch said.

Dornbusch, who correctly predicted the 1994 peso crash, unleashed a storm of controversy here recently by warning the Banco de Mexico was allowing the peso to become overvalued -- as it was before the devaluation.

He said he has not accused the central bank of intervening directly in the foreign exchange market to shore up the peso, but does blame the Banco de Mexico for encouraging peso strength this year by keeping high real interest rates in Mexico.

"I have not said that (Banco de Mexico has intervened in the currency market directly). I said that if you allow me to control the (monetary) aggregates, I control the interest rates which control the peso," he said.
Mexico's peso has fallen from about 7.60 to 7.80 per dollar in the past few sessions due in part to increasing worry about whether or not it was getting too strong.
In midday trade on Wednesday, key 48-hour contracts were off 8 centavos at 7.79/7.805 per dollar.

Dornbusch said he did not think his recent comments on the peso sparked the recent sell-off, saying that investors were concerned about high inflation in Mexico and recent news that the government decided to scale back its sell-off of the country's secondary petrochemicals industry.

"...people are uncertain about what the Pemex news really is -- is it good, or is it as one suspects, less good. I think those uncertainties have a lot more to do with it than my comments," he said before attending an Institute for International Research conference in Mexico City.
Dornbusch said the Banco de Mexico's recent tightening of liquidity in the secondary money market was aimed at calming jitters on the foreign exchange market.
But he said it should only be a temporary move and should not be aimed at helping the peso recover lost ground.
"That is alright for a very brief moment, just to stabilize expectations and to say we are not looking for a big drop ... But if they want to bring (the peso) back, that is lunacy," he said.
